Glaudell, Noble · Prime 5 A life · 1907–1972 · East St. Louis · Will County · Reedsburg, Wisconsin

Noble Glaudell
The East St. Louis Boy and the Signal Corps

↑² MM— paternal grandfather of Dana (the anchor of this page)Proven

Noble Glaudell was born on 16 February 1907 in East St. Louis, Illinois. He married Adeline Schaal at Crown Point, Indiana, in 1934, served with the 3165th Signal Service Company in the Second World War — on Saipan in 1945 — and married June Hennings in 1952. He died at Reedsburg, Wisconsin, on 5 August 1972.

1The Boy from East St. Louis

Noble Glaudell was born on the 16th of February, 1907, in East St. Louis, Illinois, across the river from St. Louis.1 The weekend he was born was a fair one — the Post-Dispatch promised moderate temperatures and westerly winds.2

He was the second child of Lee Sebastian Glaudell and Cora Esther Rainford, who had married in December 1903.3 His older sister Winona had been born in 1905; his younger brother Raymond Lee would follow in 1915.4 The family name was rare — Glaudell, sometimes spelled Glaudel — and the family was still finding its footing between Missouri and Illinois, between St. Louis and Joliet.5

His father left one paper from the Great War years. In September 1918, registering for the draft at Joliet, Lee gave his birth as the 16th of February, 1882 — his own statement of it, and a stronger witness than the 1890 his death certificate would one day claim — and wrote down as his nearest kin his brother Noble, at 108 Baker Avenue in Joliet. That was Noble August, the elder of the family's Nobles, Lee's brother and the boy's great-uncle; Joliet held him in 1918.6

His mother Cora died on the 6th of July, 1916, at St. Joseph's Hospital in Joliet, when Noble was nine.7 By 1920 he was living in the household of Walter Rainford, his mother's brother, entered as his nephew.8 A studio portrait survives of Noble at sixteen, hair combed neat, in a tie.9

Seven years after that portrait, the census-taker found him still on Will County farmland: in May 1930 Noble, twenty-three and single, was working as a farm laborer on Dixon Road in Florence Township, in the household of Daniel Hooper, his brother Raymond, fourteen, beside him — both boys entered as Hooper's "cousins." The word is the census's own: the relation column states each person's relationship to the head of the household, so the boys stand as Daniel's cousins, and the tree carries the path — Daniel's wife Lillian was a Rainford cousin of their mother's.10

Lee's life ran on past Cora's death. He married again, to Georgia R. Dean; their daughter Rita Ann was born in St. Louis on the 27th of October, 1926 — Noble's half-sister. Lee made his Social Security claim at St. Louis on the 21st of March, 1952, and was buried four days later, on the 25th of March, 1952, in Calvary Cemetery in St. Louis, Section 5, Lot S, Grave 2202. Georgia was buried in the same lot on the 2nd of April, 1963, Grave 2730.11

2Adeline

On the 18th of January, 1934, Noble married Adeline Rosella Emma Minnie Schaal at Crown Point, in Lake County, Indiana.12 She was twenty, a Kankakee County girl from the Schaal family of Bonfield.13 Their son Noble Lee was born that July; a second son, Donald Ray, followed in October 1936.14

The marriage did not last. By about 1941 Noble and Adeline had divorced — that date is an estimate, and no decree has been located.15 Adeline married Oliver Sutton in Chicago in March 1942.16 He enlisted at Chicago on 23 October 1942.

3The Signal Corps

Noble served in the Second World War with the 3165th Signal Service Company.17 The American Battle Monuments Commission's WWII Memorial Registry lists him as a World War II veteran, hometown Reedsburg, Wisconsin, honored by Fuhrman-Finnegan Post 350.17 His draft card and enlistment record survive, and the unit's history is partly known.18

The morning reports have since told the story of his training. He appears first in September 1943 — at Fort Custer, Michigan, and at the Signal Corps replacement training center at Camp Crowder, Missouri, where he completed the Powerman course that November. In the new year he moved to Fort Monmouth, New Jersey, and then, at the end of February 1944, to the Holabird Signal Depot in Baltimore. That May the depot gave him twelve days' delay en route, with permission to visit Joliet — a last trip home — before he reported to Camp Beale, California, on 4 June. There his name went onto Transfer List 354, Shipment RB 161(a), one of a company of Signal Corps men held for overseas movement; and in the first days of September 1944, under Special Orders No. 4 of the Central Pacific Base Command, he was assigned and joined at APO 958 — Honolulu — among men drawn from the 3116th Signal Service Battalion.18

For 1945 his own pages have now been pulled, and they name him month by month. In February 1945 he was transferred in grade to Detachment #17 of the 3117th Signal Service Battalion at APO 244, and the battalion's orders appointed him Technician Fifth Grade. By the 30th of June 1945 his paper had moved to Headquarters, Communications Service, and to the 3165th Signal Service Company. On the 7th of September 1945, travel orders relieved him from assignment and attached him unassigned to the Western Pacific Base Command Personnel Center and Casual Depot at APO 244, to await transport to the continental United States for discharge. The 3165th's own morning report of 18 September 1945, on Saipan, carries his name on the page that worked that relief — the page places him on Saipan with the company in its last weeks there.1920

He reached Fort Sheridan, Illinois, that autumn. Special Orders No. 101 of 25 October 1945 gave him a seven-day furlough and put him on the separation roster of 1 November, with twenty dollars' partial pay in advance. November alternated duty and furlough on the reports — out on furlough on the 6th, back and out again across the 17th, 18th, and 26th. On the 27th of November his name stands on the roster of the 1610th Company K, Separation Group 20, for the morning report of 28 November 1945 — the day of his release.19

What the company itself was doing at the end of the war, its own papers say. Month by month through the summer of 1945 the 3165th filed its war-diary report on its own letterhead — "3165th Signal Service Company, APO 244," and APO 244 was Saipan: the company ran the island's Joint Communication Center and its "Walnut" switchboard, kept up the wire plant of the whole island, and tended the submarine cable. A secret Central Pacific Base Command station list of 15 September 1945 counts the company on Saipan at twenty officers and two hundred forty-five enlisted men. What his own hands did in the 3165th — beyond the specialty the Camp Beale roster numbers 506 — the record still does not say.21

4June

In October 1952 — the 3rd, by Ancestry's reading of the Cook County index; the 4th, by FamilySearch's — Noble married again: June Margareta Hennings, in Cook County, Illinois.2223 She was twenty-seven, born in Minneapolis, Minnesota; he was forty-five.24 That Christmas they were photographed at her mother's house — Noble in a bow tie, June smiling beside him.25 The wedding day was cool and dry — a high of 64 and no rain — and the next morning a cold front swept into Chicago, the high falling to 56 under northwest winds.26

They settled in Madison, Wisconsin, in an upstairs apartment at 4649 Tonyawatha Trail, with Lake Monona just behind the house, down two flights.27 A son, Dale Eric, was born in June 1959.28 The 1950 census had caught Noble in Chicago; by the mid-sixties the Madison papers were noting his bowling league and a real-estate transaction.29 A snapshot from those years shows him in a boat, stretched out with a magazine, a handwritten caption reads: "This is the way to fish."30

5Reedsburg

Noble died on the 5th of August, 1972, in Reedsburg, Sauk County, Wisconsin, at a neighbor's home, of an apparent heart attack — in the town the Legion post called his hometown.31 The Capital Times and the Wisconsin State Journal both carried his obituary on the 7th of August.32 The day after he died, the Journal promised Reedsburg thundershowers, a high near 78, and a low of 60.33

He had come to Reedsburg in 1956. There he worked as a U.S. government inspector at Gibbs Manufacturing in Janesville, bowled in the local leagues — a 569 series made the Janesville paper in October 197134 — and belonged to the Reedsburg VFW.

June lived on for twenty-six years after him. She died on the 24th of August, 1998; her last residence was Reedsburg.24 Her burial place is not known.

The bronze tablet over him at Green Wood was June's doing. In the autumn after his death she applied for his government headstone herself — June M. Glaudell, widow, of 145 South Grove in Reedsburg, an address of hers the family papers had not held before — her signature dated the 2nd of October, 1972, asking for the flat bronze marker with its Latin cross; the marker was ordered the next July, cast by the Sheidow Bronze works. The application shows his name first typed "Nobel," then corrected by hand to NOBLE — the same wrong spelling his enlistment record bore in 1942 — and two of the government's own records at odds over his discharge, the card saying the 28th of October, 1945, the BIRLS file the 28th of November, a month apart and not yet reconciled.35

His granddaughter Dana — who never knew him as anything but "Grandpa" in the family stories — would one day write that she and her husband were the unofficial Glaudell historians, tracing the line back to Alsace-Lorraine.3637

The map

The places named in the story, from the pins placed for his life.

June lived at 145 S. Grove Street in Reedsburg; Noble is buried at Green Wood Cemetery, less than a mile away — about a 20-minute walk.
